The Responsive Manifestation of the Gold and Wood Images of Śākyamuni by Kings Udayana and Prasenajit. The Responsive Manifestation of the Gold and Wood Images of Śākyamuni by Kings Udayana and Prasenajit.
Based on the *Āgama*, the *Record of Traveling to View Buddha Images*,
the *Vinaya*, the *Biographies of the Western Regions*, the *Announcements*, and other sources, it was eight years after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni attained enlightenment.
Desiring to repay the kindness of his mother, Māyā,
he rose from the Jetavana Monastery and proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Upon a stone dais within the Hall of Good Dharma,
she sat in the full lotus posture.
At that time, Māyā—
Two streams of milk issued forth,
moistening the lips of the World-Honored One,
manifesting the karmic bond between father and son.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, the fourfold assembly in the human world could not see the Tathāgata.
They were filled with longing and sorrow,
as if they had lost their parents,
like an arrow piercing their hearts.
They went together to the place where the World-Honored One resided;
the groves, courtyards,
and halls were all empty and devoid of the Buddha.
His grief and longing redoubled,
and he could not restrain himself;
he asked Ānanda:
"Where, indeed, is the Tathāgata today?
Ānanda replied,
"I do not know."
The two kings thought of the Tathāgata and subsequently fell ill.
At that time, King Udayana...
He issued an edict to all the masters of extraordinary craftsmanship within the borders of the kingdom,
addressing them thus:
"I now wish to create a Buddha image."
The master craftsmen said to the king:
"We are unable to create the wondrous marks of a Buddha;
even if it were Viśvakarman, the god of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven..."
Yet, even if one were to perform such actions,
one could not become like the Tathāgata.
If I were to receive this mandate...
One may merely attempt to imitate a small portion of the marks such as the spiral topknot and the white tuft between the eyebrows;
however, the remaining marks, signs, radiance, and majestic virtue are impossible to equal.
Who could possibly create them?
If there should be any negligence or error regarding the images fashioned at the time the World-Honored One came to this assembly,
our names and reputations shall all universally decline and be lost.
We have deliberated together,
but none among us dared to undertake it.
We spoke again to the king, saying:
Now, for the construction of images, one should employ pure purple sandalwood that possesses a dense and compact grain and substance; however,
as for their physical forms:
"Is he seated or standing?
What are his height and proportions?
The king asked his ministers these questions.
The wise minister addressed the king, saying,
"One should fashion a seated image;
for all Buddhas [are seated]."
They attain great bodhi,
turn the wheel of the true Dharma,
and manifest great supernormal transformations.
Because they all sit while performing great Buddha-activities,
one should depict them in the form of sitting upon lion thrones in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
At that time, Viśvakarman transformed his body into that of a craftsman and took up various carving tools.
Arriving at the city gate, he said,
"I now wish to create an image for the Great King.
The king’s heart was filled with great joy.
Together with the treasurer,
he selected fragrant wood from within the inner treasury.
Carrying it upon his shoulders,
he spoke to the celestial artisan: "May you,
O Benevolent One, fashion this image."
He caused them to resemble the physical form of the Tathāgata.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana requested the Buddha’s supernormal power.
He went to have his physiognomy examined;
upon his return, he took up his axe and split a piece of wood,
the sound of which reached as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Upon arriving at the site of the Buddha's assembly,
wherever the sound of the Buddha’s power reached,
all sentient beings who heard it—
All defilements and stains shall be eliminated;
the blind shall gain sight,
and the deaf shall be able to hear.
The mute can speak;
the ugly become handsome;
the poor obtain blessings.
Even down to those in the three miserable realms, they all experience the cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness;
everything that has never before been beneficial now manifests completely.
At that time, the celestial artisan completed it in less than a day;
it was seven feet high.
Some say it is five chi;
such differences in perspective arise from varying capacities for insight.
This applies to the face as well as the hands and feet.
All were of purple-gold color.
When the king beheld their marks and signs of excellence,
pure faith arose in his heart.
They attain the patience of gentleness (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);
their karmic obstructions and afflictions are simultaneously eliminated,
with the sole exception of having previously uttered harsh words against noble beings.
At that time, King Prasenajit again summoned the skilled artisans of the kingdom,
intending to fashion a Buddha image.
And he gave rise to this thought:
"The physical form of the Tathāgata is like pure gold."
It was made entirely of *cāmikara* gold and stood five feet high.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa...
This was the beginning of these two images of the Tathāgata.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had completed the ninety-day summer retreat, he departed.
He addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:
"Seven days from now,
I shall descend to the great pond in the kingdom of Śrāvastī in Jambudvīpa."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
commanded Īśvara to construct three paths from the summit of Mount Sumeru down to the waters of the lake.
The gold, silver, and crystal are sometimes produced from the earth,
and sometimes created by the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
At that time, as the Tathāgata stepped upon the golden path,
the five kings went to where the Buddha was:
King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kāśī, and the others.
King Udayana of the country of Vatsa;
King Canda, the lord of the people of the five capitals;
and King Udayana, the lord of the Southern Sea.
King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha prostrated himself,
touching his head to [the Buddha’s] feet.
At that time, King Udayana...
Placing the Buddha image upon their heads,
they brought various supreme offerings and rare wonders to the Buddha’s presence and presented them all to the Buddha.
At that time, the wooden image rose from its seat and,
like a living Buddha, stepped through the air;
beneath its feet, rain-like flowers fell.
He emitted rays of light to welcome the World-Honored One;
with palms joined and hands crossed,
he paid homage to the Buddha, appearing somewhat like him.
And he spoke in verse:
"When the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
preaching the Dharma for his mother."
The sound of the great artisan fashioning the image was heard from afar at the Sudharmā Hall by the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
All who hear this sound shall rejoice;
those who create images in future ages will obtain immeasurable, supreme merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One likewise knelt for a long duration with palms joined toward the image,
[gazing] into the void.
Hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas likewise all joined their palms;
those images bowed their heads in person.
The World-Honored One personally touched his head with his hand and conferred this prediction upon him, saying:
"One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa,
you shall bring great benefit to humans and devas in this land."
I entrust all my disciples to you.
If there are any sentient beings...
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one creates images and uses banners,
flowers, and various incenses to make offerings,
that person, in a future life, will...
"You shall certainly see the Buddha and emerge from the suffering of birth and death.
At that time, King Udayana...
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Does the person who commissioned the image during the time of the previous Buddha's parinirvāṇa still exist in this world?"
The Buddha said:
"With my Buddha-eye, I universally behold the ten directions.
Those who fashion images after the parinirvāṇa of previous Buddhas..."
All shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions;
not a single person shall remain within the cycle of birth and death.
This applies even to those who merely fashion images of Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, he remained in the world;
this was King Bimbisāra.
At that time, there was a wooden image.
Śvetaketu said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, please proceed;
you may enter the vihāra."
The World-Honored One also spoke to the image, saying:
"Stop, stop; there is no need to speak.
My causal conditions are nearing their end."
Not long after entering parinirvāṇa,
you shall remain in the world for a long time to benefit sentient beings.
If one enters parinirvāṇa before [the Buddha],
people will treat one with contempt; if one enters after him,
people will likewise treat one with disdain.
After going back and forth several times,
the image moved forward and then returned to its original position.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One himself moved into a small vihāra beside the temple.
The image was located in a different place,
twenty paces away from [the Buddha].
King Udayana...
Overjoyed and unable to contain their happiness,
the five kings then addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"How should we construct the divine temple?"
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand,
and from within the earth emerged the temple of Kāśyapa;
he took this as the Dharma.
At that time, the five kings immediately erected a great divine temple at that very spot,
enshrined the image therein, and departed, and so forth.

2. The Second Account of the Miraculous Response of King Bimbisāra Painting an Image of Śākyamuni. This account of King Bimbisāra painting an image of Śākyamuni appears in the Vinaya-vibhaṅga. At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Veṇuvana Monastery.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there were two great cities:
the first was named Puṣpapura,
and the second was named Jayasvara.
Regarding these two cities,
they alternately experienced decline and prosperity;
at that time, the city of Jeta-vani was wealthy and flourishing.
The king's name was Śrīpatha.
He ruled the country according to the True Dharma;
there were no enemies, nor was there the suffering of illness.
The five grains flourished.
The queen’s name was Cūḍā.
He had two ministers.
The first was named Benefactor (Arthavargīya),
and the second was named Remover of Suffering (Ātaṅkavyupaśama).
At that time, the king of Rājagṛha was named Bimbisāra.
The queen's name was Vaidehī;
the crown prince's name was Ajātaśatru;
and the chief minister's name was Varṣākāra.
At that time, King Śrīmat gathered his great assembly in the morning and addressed the multitude, saying:
"Is there perhaps another country as prosperous and joyful as our own?
At that time, a merchant from the kingdom of Magadha addressed the king, saying,
"In the east, there is the city of Rājagṛha."
That country was similar to the kingdom of the king.
When the Seer heard this,
he conceived a feeling of affection for Bimbisāra.
He asked the great minister,
"What is lacking in that country?
The minister replied:
That place has no treasures.
The King filled a golden casket with exquisite jewels and dispatched a messenger along with an official edict.
He sent it to King Yaśas;
when the king read the letter and heard the news from the kingdom,
he was greatly delighted and said:
"What is lacking in that country?
The people replied,
"They have no fine cotton cloths."
At that time, the king immediately took large bolts of cloth produced in his kingdom and placed them in a chest;
he then informed King Ṛṣidatta of the aforementioned matters and sent him a letter.
In the city of Jayasvara,
King Rṣipatya saw Ānanda and asked his messenger,
"What is the king’s appearance like?"
He replied,
"His form is tall and large,
very much like that of Your Majesty."
His nature and conduct were fierce and valiant;
he personally engaged in military campaigns.
The King accordingly had five-fold superior armor fashioned for him according to his measure.
As for that which was sent by messenger:
first, when worn during the height of the heat, it becomes cool;
second, a blade cannot cut through it.
Third, it cannot be pierced by arrows.
Fourth, it avoids all poisons.
Fifth, it is able to emit light.
King Aja finished composing the edict and sent a messenger to deliver it to King Bimbisāra.
Upon reading the letter, King Bimbisāra looked at Aja.
A sense of wonder arose in his mind;
they appraised it at a value equivalent to ten billion gold coins,
which caused him deep anxiety.
"Our country has no such thing;
how shall we repay him?
At that time, the minister Vārṣika [spoke].
Seeing that the king’s countenance bore a look of sorrow, [the minister] asked for the reason.
The king answered in full detail.
The minister said:
That king presented him with only a single suit of precious armor.
Within that king’s realm dwelt the Buddha,
the wondrous jewel among men.
"In the ten directions, there is no one equal to him.
The King said,
"Truly, such a thing exists."
"What can be done about this?
The minister replied,
"One may paint an image of the World-Honored One upon a cloth."
He dispatched a messenger to deliver it in haste.
The King said,
"If that is so, inform the Buddha."
At that time, the king reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, O Subhūti! (or "Excellent, O Sumati!").
One may paint a set of Buddha images and present them to that king.
As for the method of painting these images:
first, once the images have been painted, [proceed as follows].
Below the image, write the three refuges;
next, write the five precepts,
which are the five trainings.
Next, write the forward and reverse cycles of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Above them, write two verses,
which say:
You should seek renunciation; exert yourself with diligence in the Buddha’s teaching to overcome birth and death, like an elephant pushing down a hut of grass.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya, always practice with heedfulness.
"One who can exhaust the ocean of afflictions shall reach the end of suffering.
Having finished writing this, he gave it to the messenger.
He should then report to Sīha, saying:
When you carry this painted image back to your own country,
you should hang silk banners and canopies in a spacious place,
arranging incense and flowers in profusion to create a magnificent and solemn display.
Just as he was about to open the image,
someone asked, "What is this object?
To which he replied:
This is the image of the Blessed One.
Having renounced his royal throne, he attained perfect enlightenment.
The meaning of the characters below may be explained in their proper sequence.
Then King Bimbisāra departed with joy.
He had a portrait painted depicting the circumstances of the event and collected the gold and silver caskets.

having read it, the king became enraged and addressed his ministers, saying:
It was not yet known what extraordinary or sublime objects of faith that country possessed.

"The road may be leveled and cleared for two stations by hand."
He adorned the city walls and moats with flowers,
canopies, banners, and streamers, and gathered a great multitude of people;
he then dispatched me to personally lead the fourfold army out to a great distance to welcome and receive him.
The Seer looked upon this form-spell with the intention of slighting it, saying:
"You all ought to assemble the fourfold army."
"I shall go in person to wage war against the kingdom of Magadha.

"I have heard that this king possesses great magnanimity;
one must not slight a great king.
You should now comply with his words."
The king, as instructed in the sealed letter,
provided offerings and led him to the city,
where they opened the painted image for him to gaze upon with reverence before remaining there.
At that time, merchants from the Middle Kingdom arrived together;
with one voice and in unison,
they chanted "Namo Buddhāya" and so forth.
Upon hearing this, the king’s hair stood on end all over his body.
He questioned the merchant on the meaning of each point in succession,
and the merchant answered them in full detail.
The King recited its text and returned to the palace;
there, he contemplated it according to the text until dawn, without rising from his seat.
Rejoicing at having attained the first fruit, he spoke this verse:
"Homage to the Great King of Physicians, Who skillfully cures the diseases of the mind.
Though the World-Honored One remains afar, He can cause the eye of wisdom to become clear."
He immediately sent a letter to Bimbisāra, saying:
"Relying on your benevolence, I have seen the Truths;
I wish to see the bhikṣus."
He was made to come here.
When King Bimbisāra presented the book to the Buddha,
the Buddha perceived through his supernormal knowledge that it was Kātyāyana.
Having a connection with him,
he then sent word for them to receive his instructions;
at that time, there were five hundred bhikṣus.
He went to the city of Jayapura.
At that time, Bimbisāra said to Ṛṣipatana,
"I have realized dependent origination and attained the first fruit."
He wished to see the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said,
"The five hundred bhikṣus."
He made a distant supplication,
whereupon the Master himself came to welcome him;
he then constructed a great monastery.
He constructed five hundred rooms,
thereby attaining immeasurable merit.
The Seer-Path ascetic read the book and acted exactly as it had said.
The Venerable One preached the Dharma according to their individual capacities;
some attained arhatship,
while others set out toward the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the women of the palace requested the Venerable One [to enter],
but he did not permit it, as he would not enter among women to preach the Dharma.
There was, however, a bhikṣuṇī.
"It would be appropriate to preach the Dharma for him.
The Rishi wrote a letter to inform King Bimbisāra,
and Bimbisāra reported this to the Buddha.
She dispatched five hundred nuns, including Śailā, who,
having received her instructions, went forth to preach the Dharma for her.
At that time, Lady Candraprabhā—
When his life ended, he was reborn in the heavens;
descending to earth, he startled and awakened the Great King.
The King, filled with both sorrow and joy, thought to himself:
"I shall install Prince Śikhin as king and then go forth into the religious life.
Having informed the two chief ministers of this situation, he departed.
Having heard this, the minister wept;
he took his topknot and presented it to him.
The Prince wept with grief.
The King beat the drums and rang the bells,
proclaiming throughout the land to all his subjects.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla wept aloud.
Having produced abundant wealth and treasures,
he extensively established an unrestricted assembly (paṃcavārṣika).
The king, accompanied by a single attendant, [proceeded].
He departed on foot toward the city of Rājagṛha.
Thus did the prince and the people of the land depart.
They all followed behind him as he went forward and returned;
the king gradually departed until he reached the city of Rājagṛha.
In a certain garden, he informed Bimbisāra;
having heard this, [the king] repaired the roads and led the fourfold army to the location of King Rṣipatana.
They exchanged greetings with one another,
mounted a single horse, and entered the city to inquire about his origins.
He replied that it was at the place of the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).
Desiring to seek ordination,
they immediately went together to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
His topknot hair fell off naturally,
as if he were a bhikṣu of a hundred years’ standing;
Bimbisāra prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
The *Xian Dao Biqiu* (The Bhikṣu Who Follows the Path of the Immortals) follows the multitude in his appreciation; this is merely a brief excerpt of the essential meaning. 3.

The Third Account of the Miraculous Response of the First Śākyamuni Image in the Land of Han. This account of the miraculous response of the first Śākyamuni image in the land of Han is extracted from texts such as the *Mingwang Xuanming Xiangji* (Records of Auspicious Omens of Emperor Ming). Emperor Ming of Han dreamed of a divine person.
His form hung down two zhang;
his body was the color of golden light,
and his crown was adorned with the radiance of the sun.
He questioned his ministers,
and some replied,
"There is a deity in the west."
His title was "Buddha," and his physical form was just as he had seen in the dream beneath the steps. Thereupon,
he dispatched an envoy to India.
They produced copies of the scriptures and images and presented them to the Central Kingdom,
from the Son of Heaven down to the princes and lords.
Everyone revered and served him.
Upon hearing that the spirit does not perish when a person dies,
there was none who did not become awestruck and lose their composure.
The first envoy was Cai Yi,
who brought with him the Western Region śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga and a painted image of Śākyamuni Buddha made by King Udayana.
The sovereign, regarding it as something seen in a dream,
dispatched painters to produce several copies of it.
He made offerings at the Qingliang Terrace of the Southern Palace,
at the Gaoyang Gate, and atop the Xianjie Mausoleum;
furthermore, he made offerings before the murals at Baima Monastery.
A thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry circumambulated the stupa three times;
they did the same for the image as well.
The transmission according to the Dharma is fully recorded therein. 4.

The Fourth Account of the Miraculous Response of Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty’s Invitation of a Śākyamuni Image. Regarding the miraculous response of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty’s invitation of a Śākyamuni image: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty...
On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Tianjian era,
he dreamed that a sandalwood image was entering the country;
consequently, he issued an edict to recruit those to go and welcome it.
According to the *Record of the Buddha’s Travels in India* and the two-fascicle *Sūtra of King Udayana*,
the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for one summer retreat to preach the Dharma for his mother.
The king and his ministers, desiring to behold the King of Kings, dispatched thirty-two artisans and provided sandalwood,
requesting that Mahāmaudgalyāyana employ his supernormal powers to transport them there so they might paint the likeness of the Buddha.
Having completed the illustrations as desired,
he returned and sat upon a seat five chi high at the Jetavana Monastery.
They continued to make offerings until the present day.
When the Emperor wished to invite this image [to the capital],
there were eighty men, including Huo Qian, the General Who Decides Victory, and his father Hua.
He accepted the summons and traveled there;
upon arrival, he presented a formal petition to the King of Śrāvastī, saying:
"This is an image of a celestial being from among us."
Unable to reach its limit,
he then ordered thirty-two craftsmen to further carve this sandalwood figure to create one more image.
At the hour of the Rabbit (卯), he moved his hands until the hour of the Horse (午), whereupon it was completed.
It was endowed with all the marks of excellence (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana),
and light radiated from the crown of the image's head.
A fine rain fell,
accompanied by an extraordinary fragrance.
Thus, the Udayana-rāja-sūtra says:
Since the true body has become hidden,
it manifests through two images for the universal benefit of all sentient beings.
It was Shen who performed this great service.
Qian and the others carried the second image for tens of thousands of li,
enduring every hardship as they traveled, and have reported all in detail.
Furthermore, they crossed the great ocean;
traversing wind and waves,
they were carried by the currents to a mountain.
The provisions were exhausted once more;
many among the people he led and those who escorted him perished by violence.
Encountering various fierce beasts,
he focused his mind on recitation;
then, he heard the sound of armor behind the image.
Again, he heard the sound of a bell.
Beside the cliff, there was a monk sitting upright beneath a tree.
Xuan lifted the image onto his back and placed it down before him;
the monks rose and paid homage to the image.
Xuan and the others paid their respects to the monks.
The monks gave them rinsing-water vessels and had them drink;
they all became fully satiated.
The monk said,
"This image is named Samyaksaṃbuddha;
it is King Kumbhīra."
Since arriving there, he has performed great deeds of Buddha-work;
his words were lost the moment they were spoken.
That night, everyone dreamed of a deity.
Xiao planned it together with him.
On the fifth day of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Tianjian era,
Xuan and the others arrived at the capital of Yangdu.
The Emperor traveled forty li on foot with his hundred officials to welcome [the relics] back to the Taicheng Hall.
He established a fast, ordained people, issued a general amnesty, and presented offerings. He also abolished the practice of animal sacrifice.
However, Gong Daoyu and others all constructed lotus-shaped stupas; because of this,

In the fifth month of the third year of the Taizhen era, he passed away.

He dispatched messengers from Yangdu to welcome him.

In the eighth year of the Dading era of the Later Liang,
the Daming Temple was constructed at Jingling to the north of the city.
He then returned the image to him.

The Monk Faqing of Ningguan Temple, Who Returned from the Palace of King Yama after Creating an Image of Śākyamuni. This account of the response concerning the monk Faqing of Ningguan Temple—who died after creating an image of Śākyamuni and was subsequently returned from the palace of King Yama—is extracted from the *Chuan* (Traditions).
In the third year of the Kaihuang era,
he commissioned a standing image of Śākyamuni made of lacquered cloth,
measuring sixteen feet in total height.
Before his meritorious work was completed,
Qing finished his life.
On that same day, there was also a monk named Dazhi from Baochang Temple.
After three days had passed since his death,
he also revived and went to tell the monks of the monastery, saying:
Before King Yama,
he saw that Sengfaqing had a look of sorrow;
after a short while—
Furthermore, he saw the image approach;
the king hurried forward,
descended the steps, and joined his palms in prostration before this image.
Xiang said to the King:
"Faqing is creating me;
it is not yet finished."
"How can we let him die?
The King then asked one of his attendants,
"Has Faqing been executed yet?"
He replied, "My life was not yet destined to end,
but my food supply has already been exhausted.
The king said:
"You may give him lotus leaves;
this will be his meritorious karma at the end of his life.
Suddenly, he was no longer seen.
Dazhi Suhuo recounted this to the monks of the monastery; thus,
I am now viewing it at Ningguan Temple.
In a mere moment,
he was miraculously restored to life;
what he spoke did not differ from that of the Great Wisdom.
After Faqing revived,
he constantly ate lotus leaves,
regarding them as a delicious flavor.
Furthermore, he was never permitted to eat any leftover food.
Several years after the image was installed, he passed away;
the features and proportions of that image were perfectly complete.
It frequently emits light.
Although this temple has fallen into ruin,
its image still exists today, so it is said.

6. The Sixth Account of a Miraculous Response of Deliverance from Death through the Creation of a Śākyamuni Image by the Wife of Li Tai’an of Longxi during the Tang Dynasty. This account of the miraculous response of deliverance from death through the creation of a Śākyamuni image by the wife of Li Tai’an of Longxi during the Tang Dynasty is extracted from the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Karmic Retribution). Li Tai’an of Longxi in the Tang dynasty...
Minister of Works Tai was the elder brother of Taigao.
During the Wude era, while Taigao was serving as the Governor-General of Yuezhou,
Tai went from the capital to visit him.
Tāogāo sent several servants with his elder brother to escort him back home. Upon reaching Guzhu Prefecture,
they crossed the bridge and stayed overnight at an inn.
That slave had a plot to murder Taian;
he waited until the man was fast asleep,
when the night was already past its midpoint.
The slave stabbed Tai’an in the neck with a small dagger;
the blade struck the bed,

Tài-ān woke up in alarm and called for his servant.
Those who had not rebelled [fled],

You should first take paper and brush to write a letter."
The suspended official also arrived;
he then drew his sword,

The Taian era was subsequently abolished.
Suddenly, as if in a dream,

resembling a piece of pork,

"I do not eat pork;

In front of the courtyard was a pond.

On the western bank of the pond stood a golden image.

in an instant it gradually grew larger and transformed into a monk.
Wearing his kashaya robe, which was very new and clean,
he said to Tai’an,
“I have been wounded; I shall now take this pain away for you.”
"You shall recover.
Return home, mindfully recite the Buddha's name, and cultivate goodness.
Having said this, he rubbed Tai'an's head wound with his hand and departed.
Tai’an saw this form from behind a monk;
there was a square-inch patch of red silk on his *kāṣāya*,

He was able to sit up and eat for about ten days.
The young sons of the noble families of the capital escorted him to their home.
When his family members saw him, they came to visit Tai’an and were told the circumstances of how he had been wounded.
Regarding the matter of seeing the image:
a maidservant standing to the left heard this account and remarked,

His wife sent a maidservant to an image-maker to have a Buddha statue fashioned.

there was a spot of vermilion that had stained the back of the image.

it remains in its present form,
just as you have described.
Tài'ān, together with his wife and family members,

There was no difference between them; the mark on his back was clearly that of a successor to the position.
Thereupon, he marveled at this wonder and believed that the holy teachings were indeed not in vain.

Since the Dharma first flowed eastward,

There is no such likeness as this. 7.

The Seventh Account of a Response: The Monk Shi Huijing of Wuzhen Temple Carves Images of Śākyamuni and Amitābha and Beholds the Signs of the Pure Land. New Record: The Monk Shi Huijing of Wuzhen Temple.
He was originally a native of Zizhou.
After entering the monastic order, he practiced asceticism and subsisted on a vegetarian diet;

With a heart that delighted in the Pure Land,
he personally fashioned two images of Śākyamuni and Amitābha,
making offerings to them and prostrating before them.
When I was sixty-seven years old,
on the night of the fifteenth day of the first month,
I dreamed of a person who was a śramaṇa.
His body was the color of gold.

"I only wish to see him.
"Do you still wish to see the Buddha?
He replied, "I only wish to see him."
Then the śramaṇa handed a bowl to the mirror and said,
"You should look inside the bowl.
The mirror immediately looked into the bowl.
Suddenly, he beheld a vast, magnificent, and pure land,
adorned with various jewels,
with ground of pure gold.
The paths are demarcated by golden cords;
the palaces and towers are layered upon one another in infinite succession.
Youthful devas dwell and sport therein,
as do the ocean-like assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
They surrounded the World-Honored One,
who then preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, the śramaṇas were at the forefront.
With the mirror behind him,
he gradually advanced toward the Buddha;

Suddenly the śramaṇa was no longer seen.
Jing stood with palms joined.
The Buddha said:
"Do you recognize the śramaṇa who was leading the way?
He replied, "I do not know him.
The Buddha said:
"This is the Śākyamuni image you commissioned.
Furthermore, do you recognize me?
He replied, "I do not."
He spoke again, saying:
"This Amitābha Buddha image was created by you.
Śākyamuni is like a father, and I am like a mother."
The sentient beings of the Sahā world are like infants.
It is as if a parent has many children who are young and lack understanding.
He fell into deep mud.
The father entered the deep mud and took his son in his arms.
He was placed on a high bank;
his mother remained on the bank,
holding him in her arms to nourish and raise him.
The teaching guides those who have not yet returned to the fundamental mud;
our own fundamental nature is likewise so.
Śākyamuni teaches and transforms the deluded and ignorant sentient beings of this Sahā world’s turbid and evil age.
I open the way, provide guidance,
and show them the path to the Pure Land;
I abide in that Pure Land.
Having heard these words of the Mirror, Śakrābhilagna was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
Desiring to see the Tathāgata,
he suddenly saw nothing at all;
upon waking from the dream, his body and mind were peaceful and blissful.
As if entering meditative concentration,

"Twelve years from now,
you shall be born in the Pure Land."

A monk in the neighboring room dreamed that hundreds of thousands of holy beings came from the west to welcome Huijing away.
Subtle music resounded in the air;
those who heard it all at once were indeed many. 8.

The Miraculous Response of Two Poor Men from the Kingdom of Gandhāra Each Painting a Single Image with One Gold Coin. This account of the miraculous response of two poor men from the Kingdom of Gandhāra, each using one gold coin to paint a single image together, is recorded in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions). It states that there was a painted Buddha image in the Kingdom of Gandhāra.
It is sixteen feet high;
from the chest upward,
it manifests as two distinct bodies.
From below the chest,
they were joined into a single body.
According to what the elders have heard, it was said:
In the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself through his own labor;
he obtained a single gold coin.
He wished to create an image of the Buddha and said to a painter,
"I now desire to depict the wondrous features of the Tathāgata."
There was a single gold coin;
it was still insufficient to reward his merit.
His long-standing mind had been anxious over poverty, and he was now pressed by destitution.
At that time, the painter,
moved by his utmost sincerity,
said nothing regarding the price.
He was permitted to succeed.
Furthermore, there was another person whose circumstances were identical to those previously described.
Carrying a single coin,
he sought to have an image of the Buddha painted;
at that time, the painter accepted the money from the two men.
They sought exquisite pigments and together painted a single image;
the two of them worked on the same day.
They both came together to pay their respects.
The painter pointed to a single image and,
showing it to the two men, said to them:
"This is your Buddha image.
The two looked at each other as if harboring something in their hearts.
The painter, knowing their suspicion in his heart,
said to the two men:
"Why do you reflect so long?"
Whatever objects were received,
not even a hair’s breadth was diminished;
these words are not false.
The image must have manifested a divine transformation;
before the sound of his voice had even faded,
the image displayed a supernatural marvel.
As their divided bodies intermingled their shadows and their radiant forms illuminated one another,
the two men were filled with joy and submission.
His heart was filled with faith and joy. 9.

The Ninth Account of the Response of Yu Anliang of Yuyang County, Youzhou, in the Tang Dynasty, Who Aided Another in Creating a Statue of Śākyamuni and Was Thus Released from Suffering. Yu Anliang of Yuyang County, Youzhou, in the Tang Dynasty, aided another person in creating a statue of Śākyamuni Buddha and thereby experienced a response that delivered him from suffering. Yu Anliang of Yuyang County, Youzhou...
His surname was Yu.
His family made their living by slaughtering living beings; this was the very occupation he practiced.
They do not know how many thousands of millions there are,
nor do they recognize the cultivation of merit;
they constantly say:
Those who cultivate goodness will inevitably decline.
He lived to the age of thirty-seven;
while out hunting, he fell from his horse.
He fainted and his breath was suddenly exhausted;
only after half a day did he revive.
Rising up, he wept bitterly and threw himself upon the great earth.
He repented before the Pure Heaven, saying, "I was mistaken!
I was mistaken!
When his servants asked him the reason for this, he replied:
After a long while, he said,
"When I first fainted,
there were two beings with the heads of horses and oxen."
Fire chariots come and cast me into my own body;
fierce flames burn my body,
causing immeasurable suffering and pain.
At that time, there was a person dressed in monastic robes who came and sprinkled water upon the cart and used his hands to ward off the fire.
The suffering of body and mind ceased.
Arriving at the abode of King Yama,
the Dharma King, he saw the śramaṇa.
He descended the steps at a run,
joined his palms in reverence, and said:
"For what reason have you come to sit here?"
The monk said,
"This sinner is my patron;
I wish to beg for his life for a short while."
The king said,
"He is an evil man;
he must not be released to return."
"However, since the Great Master has come here for such a purpose, it would be regrettable to lose him.
The monk will take me back.
The man of good conscience felt doubt and wonder.
"I do not understand what you mean by 'assist me.
Who is it that asks the Saṃgha?
They replied:
"Do you not recognize him?
Your elder brother, An-tong, has resolved his mind on enlightenment and is creating an image of Śākyamuni."
"You have contributed thirty coins based on this condition to assist in the creation of that image;
since you have contributed a small amount of money, you shall have an image of me made."
"For this reason, I have come to rescue you.
Look at these colored robes as proof.
Having spoken, he vanished.
For these reasons, he repented his transgressions with sorrowful self-reproach,
and then went to the home of An Tong.
The elder brother’s image was exactly as he had seen it;
moved by this realization,
he donned the robes and fashioned the image himself.

10. The Tenth Account of the Monk Dharmaruci from the Kingdom of Saṃkāśya in Northern India, Who Was Struck with Awe by a Manifestation of the Śākyamuni Image, as Recorded in the *Changmin Youli Ji* (Record of the Wandering of the Monk Changmin). The monk Changmin made a great vow.
Traveling far to the west to pay homage to the Tathāgata’s traces of his past deeds,
he arrived at the kingdom of Saṃkāśya in North India.
There is a stone stupa over twenty zhang in height,
beside which stands a new vihāra containing carved sandalwood images of Śākyamuni and Maitreya seated.
If one prays with a sincere heart,
it will certainly manifest its wondrous form to announce good or ill fortune;
this tradition originated with the elders of old.
Several decades ago,
there was a bhikṣu whose name in Sanskrit was Bandhudatta.
In the Tang language, this is called Faa (Dharmapriya).
She lived beside a stone stupa and made a vow to create an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa from a foreign land who stayed overnight in the Fayi (Dharma-Love) quarters and praised the profound meaning of the Buddha’s sutras.
Aiwen was delighted and,
recounting their mutual longings, said:
"I wish to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven and shall therefore create an image of Maitreya.
The śramaṇa said:
If one makes a vow to be reborn in Tuṣita,
one should fashion an image of Śākyamuni;
Maitreya is a disciple of Śākyamuni.
Those who have attained liberation through the three assemblies,
and the disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma—
if one has the power to do so.
One should fashion two images;
if one lacks the capacity,
one should first fashion that of Śākyamuni.
The reason for this is that these three realms now all belong to the Great Teacher.
He declared of himself,
"I alone am able to provide protection.
How can you not reflect upon his debt of gratitude?
Ai said, "Since Śākyamuni has entered nirvana,
there will be no future transformation."
How could they assist those about to be born?
Firmly clinging [to their views] and refusing to change,
each lay down to sleep.
The night grew even clearer;
his sleep was suddenly broken by awakening,
and he wept bitterly, casting his five limbs upon the ground.
A śramaṇa from a foreign land asked about the origins [of this].
He replied:
"In my dream, I saw a golden-bodied person over ten feet tall."
He then addressed him with gentle words, saying:
"You are my disciple;
you have been under my guidance and training for a long time."
It is erroneously said that [the self] is eternally extinguished;
in truth, it is permanently abiding and does not perish.
Now, these three realms are all mine.
Sentient beings do not realize this in their daily lives:
that within the three realms, from the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and lands,
as well as the space itself, all grains, wheat, and so forth consumed by sentient beings [are produced through the power of their karma].
"All these are things my own body has performed as a counter-measure.
The Buddhas of the ten directions assist me in this transformation;
how can you treat it with such contempt and refuse to create an image?"
If you do not create my image,
you will ultimately be unable to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven;
for you have thus slighted your teacher.
If Master Hui praises it,
one may not go to the pure lands of the ten directions;
may all Buddhas assist me.
"Is it that you wish to slight me by speaking these words in such a hidden and obscure manner?
At that time, there was a foreign śramaṇa.
Nor does it go anywhere,
yet suddenly it is no longer seen;
this is the sorrowful grief of attachment to dharmas.
Having relinquished their robes, alms bowls,
and personal belongings, they fashioned these two images;
the vihāra was constructed by the people of the country collectively.
He stayed for many days out of compassion, and after making his requests, he departed, it is said. 11.

The Eleventh Account of the Response to the Request of the Bodhisattva with Five Supernatural Powers at Kukkutapāda Monastery to Have Amitābha Buddha Depicted. The account of the response to the request of the Bodhisattva with Five Supernatural Powers at Kukkutapāda Monastery to have Amitābha Buddha depicted is cited from the *Gantong lu* (Records of Spiritual Resonance), which quotes the *Xiyu zhuan* (Account of the Western Regions). It is traditionally transmitted as follows:

In the past, a Bodhisattva possessing the five supernatural powers at the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery in India traveled to the Land of Ultimate Bliss to invite Amitābha Buddha to [welcome] the sentient beings of the Sahā world.
If one wishes to be born in the Pure Land but there is no image of the Buddha,
one’s power of aspiration has no means by which it may be realized.
"Please grant us your permission.
The Buddha said,
"You may go on ahead for now."
Soon he will appear there;
and when the Bodhisattva returns,
that image will have already arrived.
One Buddha and fifty bodhisattvas each sat upon lotus flowers atop the leaves of trees.
The Bodhisattva took the leaf where it was located and had it painted and circulated far and wide. 12.

The Twelfth Account of the Miraculous Response of the Venerable Amitāyus Image Painted by the Śramaṇa Huǐhǎi of Ānle Monastery during the Sui Dynasty. The account of the miraculous response of the venerable Amitāyus image painted by the Śramaṇa Huǐhǎi of Ānle Monastery in Jiangdu during the Sui Dynasty appears in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) compiled during the Tang Dynasty. The Śramaṇa Huǐhǎi of Ānle Monastery in Jiangdu [was as follows].
His secular surname was Zhang,
and he was a native of Wucheng in Qinghe.
He was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras.
However, as he took the Pure Land as his primary practice,
his single-minded devotion moved the divine.
Suddenly, there appeared a monk from Qizhou named Daoling.
He brought an image of Amitāyus and said,
"This was a Bodhisattva with the five supernatural powers from the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery in India,
who traveled through the air to that World of Peace and Bliss."
Having depicted his countenance,
he found a profound resonance with his long-held aspirations and felt deep devotion toward ritual repentance.
Thereupon, he beheld a divine radiance, brilliantly blazing;
his hopes were fulfilled beyond expectation,
and thus he was liberated from suffering through this imitation.
He vowed to be reborn in that land,
keeping this in mind until the end of his days.
One night, he suddenly rose from his seat.
He remained seated in the lotus posture with his face constantly turned toward the west;
he passed away at dawn.
His countenance was serene and harmonious,
as if a deity were present.
He was sixty-nine years of age.

13. The Thirteenth Account of a Miraculous Response Concerning the Three-Inch Amitābha Image of the Sui Monk Daoyu. This account of the miraculous response of the three-inch Amitābha image of the Sui monk Daoyu is recorded in the *Ruiying zhuan* (Account of Auspicious Responses). Regarding the Sui monk Daoyu:
At Kaibō-ji Temple,
he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and fashioned a sandalwood image three inches in height.
Later, Daoyu suddenly died;
after seven days had passed, he revived and said:
"At first, I saw a worthy man."
Having been reborn at the edge of the precious pond,
the wise one circumambulated the flower three times,
and the flower immediately blossomed.

Yuyao circumambulated the flower three times, but it would not open;
he then reached out his hand and pushed at the flower.
The flowers withered and fell.
Amitābha Buddha said,
"Return for now to that land."
Confess all transgressions and bathe in fragrant water;
when the morning star appears, I shall come to welcome you.
"You have fashioned my image;
why is it so small?
The artisan replied:
If the mind is great, it is great;
if the mind is small, it is small.
Having spoken thus, the image pervaded all of space.
He immediately bathed in fragrant water and,
with single-minded repentance,
said to the multitude:
This serves as an analogy for mindfulness of the Buddha:
when the morning star appears,
the transformation Buddhas come to welcome one.
The multitude witnessed the radiance and all heard it;
they immediately passed away.
At that time, it was the eighth year of the Kaihuang era.

14. The Fourteenth Account of the Miraculous Response of Zhang Yuanshou of Bingzhou, Who Created an Image of Amitābha for His Deceased Relative. This account of Zhang Yuanshou of Bingzhou creating an image of Amitābha for his deceased relative appears in the *Bingzhou ji* (Records of Bingzhou). Zhang Yuanshou was a native of Bingzhou.
Although he possessed a virtuous mind,
his family made their living by killing living beings;
subsequently, both his parents passed away.
Thereafter, he renounced the karma of taking life and practiced the mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha,
vowing to save his parents.
He fashioned a three-foot image of Amitābha Buddha and installed it in his former chamber,
where he offered incense, flowers, and lamps.
He made offerings and prostrated.
In his dream, there was light within the room;
within that light were more than twenty people riding upon lotus pedestals.
Among them, two men approached the courtyard and called out to Yuanshou.
Yuanshou immediately asked, "Who is it?"
He replied, "I am your father and mother;
although I have attained the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha,
I am fond of wine and meat."
Because he killed many fish, birds, and other creatures,
he fell into the Raurava Hell; yet,
even though he had fallen into hell...
By the power of mindfulness of the Buddha,
molten iron and copper became like cool water;
yesterday, the śramaṇa’s body was three feet tall.
He preached the Dharma.
More than twenty fellow practitioners heard the śramaṇa’s teaching.
They all departed from the hells and were reborn in the Pure Land.
At that time, Śāriputra informed [the Buddha] of these causes and conditions.
Those who are in the air are those with similar karma within the hells.
Having explained this matter, [he continued].
He pointed toward the west and departed.
He told the monks about his dream,
and they all said that it referred to the image he had commissioned.
He went into the hells to rescue those suffering in misery. 15.

The response of Shi Daoru creating an image of Amitābha to rescue sentient beings in the three evil paths is recorded in the *Bingzhou ji* (Record of Bingzhou). they make vows to rescue sentient beings of the three miserable realms from their suffering.
I fashioned a sixteen-foot golden image of Amitābha;

While in the dream before the image,
a certain official of the underworld appeared,
holding a golden paper document that read:
"This is the document of the King of Dharma, Yama,

As it says when one opens and looks upon it:

their resolve becomes even more focused upon awakening from the dream.
On the days of the fast, light emanated from the chest of the image;

or so it appeared in someone's dream.
The Way manifests as the golden-colored body;

or preaches the Dharma for hungry ghosts.

Since such instances of spiritual resonance are so numerous, one may know with certainty that his vows will not be in vain. 16. The Sixteenth Account of Spiritual Resonance: The Śramaṇa Shi Sengao of the Song Dynasty Carves a Six-Foot Image of Amitāyus.

This account of the Śramaṇa Shi Sengao of Changsha Temple in Jiangling, Song, carving a six-foot image of Amitāyus, is excerpted from the *Liang Dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), having been selected for its essential meaning from the "Pearl Forest" (*Zhulin*). Those who beheld it were moved to tears of faith, and many attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thus, the efficacy of his devotion was manifest. This concludes the sixteenth account.
With a resolute character fierce and stern, he aspired toward the Western Land;

Hearing that the temple on Mount Tongxi in Xiangzhou possessed numerous bronze ritual vessels,
he wished to convert and guide the ghosts and spirits by means of them.
He took [the items] to fulfill the requirements.

informed the plaintiff Yuan.

moreover, as the barbarians guarded them,

the deity already knew it in advance;
the wind shook and the clouds darkened.
The birds and beasts cried out;
in an instant, the height was reached.
The mist cleared and the sun shone bright.
Before reaching the temple building,
at a distance of more than twenty paces,
there were two bronze cauldrons.
Each measured several hundred hu;
there he saw a great serpent over ten zhang in length.
He leaped out from the cauldron,
his body stretching across the path;
he was followed by a hundred attendants.
They all retreated and dispersed.
Daogao then ordered his robes to be donned and proceeded forward,
shaking his mendicant’s staff.
He said to the snake,
"Because of the karmic offenses of your previous lives, you have been reborn as a python and have not heard of the Triple Gem."
By what means can one extricate oneself?
I have fashioned a sixteen-foot image of Amitāyus;
hear this sound of the bronze gong.
"You have come from afar to visit me;
I hope you will make way so that I may pass.
The snake then raised its hood.
Seeing this, Gao drew his body away and departed.
Gao personally led his followers and swiftly seized the bronze vessels.
There was only a spittoon by the bedside,
which could hold about four *sheng*;
the wall-crawling insects were over a foot long.
He leaped about as he entered and exited,
eventually leaving them behind and not taking them;
among the temple vessels, which were heavy and large, he did not take even one.
Only those who were slightly superior returned with their boats full.
The person guarding the temple—
The local tribes dared not resist or push him back.
Daogao returned to the capital and cast the image,
completing the work in the ninth year of the Yuanshou era.
The deity’s appearance is dignified and majestic,
its radiant splendor magnificent and brilliant;
the fame of the miraculous manifestations of this image has spread far and wide.

17. The Seventeenth Response from the Kingdom of Anxi, Induced by Amitābha Buddha’s Transformation into a Parrot. This response concerning Amitābha Buddha’s transformation into a parrot to induce [the Dharma] in the Kingdom of Anxi appears in the *Wai Guo Ji* (Records of Foreign Countries). Dwelling in a remote region, his nature was coarse and his spirit dull.

its color golden with markings of blue and white.

Someone asked, "What do you take as food?

"My body is stout and my strength is great.
If you wish to nourish me,
you may chant the name of the Buddha."
The people all sang together in competition.
The bird gradually flew up into the air and then returned to stay on the ground.
The bird said:
"Do you wish to see a land of abundance?
They replied, "We wish to see it.
The bird said:
"If you wish to see [him], you must ride upon my wings.
When the people mounted his wings,
their strength was still somewhat weak.
The bird exhorted him to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;

From that time onward...
The people of Anxi had little knowledge of the Buddha-dharma,

18. The Eighteenth Response of Amitābha Buddha Manifesting as a Great Fish to Entice Fishermen. To the southwest of the kingdom of Śrīvijaya (Zhíshīzǐ Guó), one looks out for many miles without knowing its limit.

Each person spoke in human speech,
chanting "Namo Amitābha Buddha.
When the sailors saw this, they were amazed.
Not understanding the reason for this,
they merely rely on the chanting of the words and call it the "A-mi-t'o fish."
Someone was chanting "Amitābha," and as the fish gradually approached the shore,

The meat was extremely delicious.
If those people had chanted for a long time,

The flavor of meat is supreme;

Three months after his life ended,

arriving at the shore of the sea islet.
He addressed the people, saying,
"I was the eldest among the fishermen;
at the end of my life, I was reborn in the world of Ultimate Bliss."
That great fish was manifested by the Tathāgata Amitābha;

Deeply stained by passion,

"The disciple shall certainly attain rebirth there.
